\chapter{Case Endings and Dative Subjects}
\label{ch:ml-dative-case}

This chapter is generated from the canonical micro-lessons used by Language Ladder.
Each section stays independently resumable and preserves the authored prerequisite order.

\section[-ikku]{-\ml{ിക്ക്} (-ikku) — "to, for"}

\label{lesson:ML-C06-dative-ikku}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Your first \textbf{case ending}. English puts "to" in \textbf{front} as its own word. Malayalam sticks it on the \textbf{back} — and that is the biggest structural fact about the language.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{+ dative} & \textbf{meaning} \\
\midrule
\ml{പേര്} \emph{pēru} — name & \ml{പേര}\textbf{\ml{ിന്}} \emph{pēr\textbf{inu}} & to/for the name \\
\ml{ജോലി} \emph{jōli} — work & \ml{ജോലി}\textbf{\ml{ക്ക്}} \emph{jōli\textbf{kku}} & for work \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Malayalam's dative has two shapes — \textbf{-\ml{ിക്ക്}} \emph{-ikku} and \textbf{-\ml{ിന്}} \emph{-inu} — chosen by the sound the noun ends in. Same case, same job; the seam is still visible.

And with "I", which reshapes first:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ}} \emph{ñān} ("I") $\to$ \textbf{\ml{എനിക്ക്}} \emph{enikku} ("to me")
\end{quote}

Learn \emph{enikku} cold — it opens a great many everyday Malayalam sentences, as the next lesson shows.

\begin{culture}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{Malayalam \textbf{-ikku}} & \textbf{a Latin ending like \textbf{-īs}} \\
\midrule
pins down the case? & \textbf{yes} — dative, always & \textbf{no} — \emph{-īs} is dative \textbf{or} ablative \\
carries number? & \textbf{no} — a separate suffix does & yes — plural, baked in \\
carries declension class? & \textbf{no} & yes — 1st/2nd only \\
can you see the seam? & \textbf{yes}: \emph{jōli} + \emph{kku} & no — one fused lump \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Malayalam \textbf{stacks}: each suffix means one thing and sits in a fixed order — so a long word can be read piece by piece. Latin \textbf{fuses}: \emph{-īs} is case \emph{and} plural \emph{and} declension at once, indivisible, and it doesn't even settle \emph{which} case. Malayalam's dative is never ambiguous.

That's what "\textbf{agglutinative}" means, and why Malayalam words grow long without growing hard: they are \textbf{built}, not memorised.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "\emph{pēru} … \emph{pērinu}"{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "\emph{ñān} … \emph{enikku}" — "I" … "to me"{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "\emph{jōlikku}" — "for work," from Ch. 5's \ml{ജോലി}{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the principle — "one suffix, one meaning, visible seam"{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What does \textbf{-\ml{ിക്ക്}} mean? ("\textbf{To}" or "\textbf{for}.") Where does it go? (\textbf{On the end} of the noun.) What is "to me"? (\textbf{\ml{എനിക്ക്}} \emph{enikku}.) Why does the suffix have two shapes? (\textbf{-ikku} and \textbf{-inu} are chosen by the noun's ending — one case, two forms.) How is that unlike a Latin ending? (Latin \textbf{fuses} case+number+declension — and \emph{-īs} doesn't even fix \emph{which} case; Malayalam's carries \textbf{one} meaning, unambiguously, seam visible.) Next: the sentence where the person isn't the subject.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[enikku malayāḷam aṟiyām]{\ml{എനിക്ക്} \ml{മലയാളം} \ml{അറിയാം} — "I know Malayalam"}

\label{lesson:ML-C06-dative-subject}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Chapter 5 gave you \textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{മലയാളം} \ml{സംസാരിക്കുന്നു}} — "\textbf{I} speak Malayalam." Now say "I \textbf{know} Malayalam." Malayalam will not let you use \emph{ñān}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{എനിക്ക്} \ml{മലയാളം} \ml{അറിയാം}.} \emph{enikku malayāḷam aṟiyām.} literally: "\textbf{to-me} Malayalam is-knowable."
\end{quote}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{piece} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{എനിക്ക്}} \emph{enikku} & "to me" — the dative from the last lesson \\
\textbf{\ml{മലയാളം}} \emph{malayāḷam} & Malayalam (Ch. 5) \\
\textbf{\ml{അറിയാം}} \emph{aṟiyām} & "can be known" — \emph{aṟiy-} "know" + \textbf{-ām}, the \emph{able-to} ending \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{You are not the subject.} \emph{Ñān} is gone; the person has been moved into the dative, and the sentence is now about the \textbf{language}. Malayalam isn't saying you perform an act of knowing — it's saying the language is knowable \textbf{to you}.

\begin{cousinweb}
Malayalam separates what you \textbf{do} from what \textbf{happens to} you. Speaking is an action, so Ch. 5 used \emph{ñān}. But knowing, liking, wanting, being hungry — these \textbf{arrive} at you. Malayalam marks that by putting the person in the \textbf{dative}.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{English frames it as} & \textbf{Malayalam frames it as} \\
\midrule
I \textbf{know} Malayalam & Malayalam is known \textbf{to me} \\
I \textbf{like} it & it is pleasing \textbf{to me} \\
I \textbf{am} cold & cold is \textbf{to me} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

English preserves one fossil of exactly this: "\textbf{methinks}" — \emph{me} is a dative, "it seems \textbf{to me}." Malayalam made it the rule.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{cousinweb}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{language} & \textbf{"I know {[}the language{]}"} & \textbf{the dative} \\
\midrule
Malayalam & \emph{enikku malayāḷam aṟiyām} & \textbf{-ikku} \\
Tamil & \emph{enakku tamiḻ teriyum} & \textbf{-ukku} \\
Telugu & \emph{nāku telugu vaccu} & \textbf{-ku} \\
Kannada & \emph{nanage kannaḍa gottu} & \textbf{-ge} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Look at the first column: Malayalam's \emph{enikku} and Tamil's \emph{enakku} are nearly the \textbf{same word} — the two languages separated most recently of the four, and it shows. One construction, four languages, four visibly related suffixes: the Dravidian family showing its bones, as \emph{blanc/bianco/branco} did for Romance.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "\emph{enikku malayāḷam aṟiyām}"{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the contrast — "\emph{ñān malayāḷam saṁsārikkunnu}" (I speak) … "\emph{enikku malayāḷam aṟiyām}" (known to me){]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the near-twins — "\emph{enikku} … \emph{enakku}"{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the four cousins — "\emph{-ikku · -ukku · -ku · -ge}"{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What does \textbf{\ml{എനിക്ക്} \ml{മലയാളം} \ml{അറിയാം}} literally say? ("\textbf{To-me} Malayalam \textbf{is-knowable}.") What has English got that Malayalam hasn't? (A nominative "\textbf{I}" — \emph{ñān} is replaced by the dative \emph{enikku}.) Why the dative? (Knowing \textbf{happens to} you.) Which Tamil word is \emph{enikku} almost identical to, and why? (\textbf{Enakku} — Tamil and Malayalam split most recently of the four.) Which English word keeps the same idea? (\textbf{Methinks}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
